title: Fear, outrage grow as Quebec moves to ban religious symbols for elementary students
summary: Quebec parents of young children who wear religious symbols are worried about the new PQ government’s proposal to ban elementary school students from wearing such symbols at school. Experts say there…

image.caption: Mehwaish Raja's 11-year-old daughter started wearing a hijab to elementary school this fall. Raja says she doesn't think the government should decide what her daughter wears to school. (Steve Rukavina, CBC News)

blocks.text: Mehwaish Raja’s 11-year-old daughter surprised her during a conversation this past summer on the way to day camp.
“She shared with me during the car ride: ‘Mama, I will wear my hijab at the end of the summer,’” Raja said.
Up until that point, her daughter only wore the hijab for special occasions, and Raja had never insisted she wear it regularly.
“I just said, ‘OK.’ And by the end of the summer, it actually happened,” Raja said.
Her daughter now wears the hijab every day in her Grade 5 class in a public school in Montreal’s West Island.
Now, the new Parti Québécois government is proposing a law that would make that practice illegal as part of a series of measures announced on the campaign trail to strengthen secularism.

items: Groups decry Quebec's proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols

blocks.text: Raja is struggling to understand why.
“Honestly, I'm out of words. I'm out of words when I hear things like this,” she said.
She doesn’t think the government should be able to decide what her daughter wears to school.
“When we step out of our house, we leave as who we are. What part of us do we leave at home?” she said.
Parents, experts raise concerns over Quebec’s proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols
Religious symbols gradually squeezed out of schools

The previous CAQ government already introduced several laws restricting religious symbols in schools, preventing at first teachers, and then all school staff – even parent volunteers – from wearing them.

Generally, religious symbols bans in Quebec have targeted employees of the state considered to be in positions of authority, but the CAQ opened the door to targeting students by introducing a ban on full face coverings at school.
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is opening that door wider, proposing a blanket ban preventing elementary school students from wearing "conspicuous" religious symbols while at school.

“Separating children through what they wear and through religious beliefs at such a young age is not helping cohesion and integration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in September when announcing the measure, without providing any specific examples.
“We think it's a good policy in terms of letting children just be children, with no connection whatsoever to what their parents believe about religion,” he'd said.

When proposing the religious ban for elementary schools during the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the symbols 'interfere with cohesion and integration.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)
Winning a minority government in the general election did not soften the PQ's resolve, with new Education Minister Joël Arseneau saying the measure was a "non-negotiable."
"It’s on this basis that we were elected, and it’s on this basis that we’re working,” Arseneau told reporters at the National Assembly in late October.
Mother says proposed law based on misconceptions
Asma Qureshi says the PQ's proposal comes from a place of ignorance.

Qureshi, who lives on Montreal’s South Shore, has four children. Her oldest daughter, now in high school, started wearing a hijab to school when she was in Grade 4. Her youngest daughter, currently in kindergarten, wore one to school a couple of times this year just to try it.
Qureshi – who wears a hijab herself – says in both cases, she didn’t ask or order her daughters to wear one.
"I told myself that I would never impose it on my kids," she said.
"There’s this narrative that goes around – and it's been there since I was a young kid – that children and women are being forced to wear the scarf."

items: Quebec’s secularism laws upended their lives. They fear what comes next could be worse

blocks.text: Qureshi thinks that misconception is what’s feeding the gradual tightening of restrictions on wearing religious symbols in Quebec, particularly in schools.
She says she hasn’t yet discussed the proposed ban with her daughters.
“How do you tell a child it’s against the law for you to wear something that your mother wears?” she said.
Raja says her daughter's decision to start wearing the hijab regularly this fall convinced her to do the same. (CBC News)
For Raja, who up until now had been reluctant to wear a hijab in Quebec for fear of standing out, says her daughter's decision to wear one at school this fall convinced her to do the same.
“I'm really proud of her because at 11 years old, she decided to wear it, whereas I’m 40 and I hadn't been able to,” she said.
“My daughter truly inspired me."
Ban would cause harm, experts say
Experts in secularism and child development told CBC there is no justification for banning students from wearing religious symbols — and that the measure would be harmful.

Thomas Dee, an economist at Stanford University who specializes in how education policy affects student outcomes, disagreed with the notion of asking children to leave their parents' religious baggage behind.
“Parents are children's first and most impactful teachers, and to sideline their guidance and insights just seems misguided to me and disrespectful,” he said.
Dee testified as an expert witness in the court challenge to Bill 21, Quebec’s first secularism law.

Thomas Dee, an economics professor at Stanford University who studies the effects of education policy on student outcomes, says a policy that marginalizes parents' values in school is misguided and disrespectful. (CBC News)
Sivane Hirsch, a professor in the faculty of education at Université Laval who specializes in cultural and religious diversity in schools, believes the ban is a horrible idea.
“We don’t want children to feel they’re being taught in school against their parents, against their family,” Hirsch said.
Dee said such a conflict would also hurt students’ performance.
“Anything that makes students feel less welcome or less at ease will imply they're not able to bring their full attention and motivation to the realization of their academic potential,” Dee said.

items: Gatineau mom told she can't wear hijab at after-school event: parent committee

blocks.text: Zeinab Diab, a religious studies researcher at Université de Montréal and author of Au nom de la laïcité, a book about Islamophobia in Quebec, said a secularism law that targets young children is inhumane.
“They are dehumanizing them and limiting their access to school. What kind of society allows that?” she said.
Author and religious studies researcher Zeinab Diab says targeting children for a religious symbols ban is inhumane. (CBC News)
Dee said the presence of religious symbols in the classroom could actually help.
“If you engage with people across difference, you no longer use simple rules of thumb to judge them, but rather you judge them as people,” he said.
Qureshi said that was her daughter’s experience.
She said no other students made negative comments or gave her daughter a hard time when she started wearing the hijab.
“It was just like she was any other regular person,” she said. “That's the beautiful thing – when people can recognize you for who you are rather than what you wear."
PQ needs support of at least 1 other party
In order to adopt the ban, the PQ will need support from at least one other party in the National Assembly.
Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberals and the Official Opposition, said last week his party wouldn’t support the measure.
“We're talking about children. I'm not going to do politics on the backs of children,” Milliard said.
Québec Solidaire also doesn’t support the measure.
That leaves the Conservative Party of Quebec.
On Monday, leader Éric Duhaime said his party generally supports secularism, but wanted to see more details before deciding whether to support the proposed law.
"I mean, what are we going to do with those kids if they don't respect the rules?" Duhaime told reporters.
"That's the kind of thing that I want to know before we move forward."
Education Minister Joël Arseneau says he's negotiating with other parties about the idea of banning religious symbols for elementary school students, and that their positions may evolve. (CBC News)
Last week, Arseneau said he was in negotiations with other parties about the bill, and that their positions may evolve. He declined CBC’s request for an interview.
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association issued a statement Tuesday calling on all members of the National Assembly to oppose the idea regardless of of their political affiliation.

"Children’s access to education should never be conditional on whether the government approves of their religious identity or expression," Harini Sivalingam, director of equality for the CCLA, said in the statement.
"Schools should be places where children learn, develop their identities and build relationships with others from different backgrounds," Sivalingam said.
"You cannot promote inclusion by excluding children,” she said.
Raja says if the ban does become law, her daughter would likely leave her current school.
“If the public system is really asking us not to practise certain values that we strongly believe in, I would choose another way of educating my children,” she said.
For her that would likely be private school, but she said some other parents might choose homeschooling.
Diab said not all families have either the money or the time for those options.
“Maybe they’re going to adapt, but no one should be always in fight and survival mode,” she said.
“This is exhausting.”
